claim: Tsafrir (2006 thesis, chapter 4): runtime predictions used without a correction step worsened backfilling performance by up to an order of magnitude ('performance is worsened by up to an order of magnitude!').
note: Thesis text, not the TPDS 2007 paper, which did not download.

claim: Tsafrir (2006 thesis, chapter 4): exploiting more history to predict job runtimes made backfilling performance worse ('the more history we exploit when making a prediction, the worse the resulting performance becomes').
note: Thesis text, not the TPDS 2007 paper.

claim: Tsafrir (2006 thesis, citing another study of five supercomputers over eleven years): average utilization of 40-60 % went up to around 70 % once backfilling was introduced; a before-and-after observation, not a controlled comparison.
note: Narrowed after refute A60: the cause is not isolated. The figure is from the cited study, as the thesis states it (txt lines 667-668).

claim: Tsafrir (2006 thesis): backfilling was shown to be a close second to more sophisticated algorithms that use preemption, migration or dynamic partitioning.

Tsafrir (2006 thesis): the runtime predictor used is the average runtime of the same user's two most recently submitted, already terminated jobs ('averaging the runtime of the two most recently submitted (and already terminated) jobs by the same user').

Tsafrir (2006 thesis, Table 4.3, simulation replay of four real logs, not a live system): EASY++ cut average job wait versus EASY by 10 % (SDSC, 363 to 327 min), 33 % (CTC, 21 to 14 min), 17 % (KTH, 114 to 95 min) and 33 % (BLUE, 130 to 87 min).
note: Collect line gives SDSC 363 to 327 as -10 %; the minute values are copied from the same line.

claim: Tsafrir (2006 thesis, Table 4.3, simulation replay of four real logs, not a live system): EASY++ cut bounded slowdown versus EASY by 29 % (SDSC, 99 to 70), 37 % (CTC, 4.6 to 2.9), 36 % (KTH, 90 to 57) and 47 % (BLUE, 35 to 19).
Tsafrir (2006 thesis): shortest-job-backfilled-first alone gave typical improvements of 10-20 %, and up to 42 % (BLUE's bounded slowdown).
note: A figure from the thesis text, not from Table 4.3.

claim: Tsafrir (2006 thesis): the EASY+ variant's typical improvement over vanilla EASY is around 25 %.
Tsafrir (2006 thesis): making users' runtime estimates less accurate by doubling them ('X2') tends to help backfilling.
note: The original Mu'alem and Feitelson paper was not opened; the thesis is the only source here.

claim: Tsafrir (2006 thesis): runtime over estimate accuracy was 31 to 47 % with users' estimates and about 60 % with EASY++.
Tsafrir (2006 thesis): EASY++ outperforms the doubled-estimate variant X2 by a wide margin for all traces and both metrics.
Kolisch and Hartmann (2006, EJOR): the parameters of activity durations and resource demands are assumed to be nonnegative and deterministic ('assumed to be nonnegative and deterministic').
note: A stated condition: durations are known exactly.

claim: Kolisch and Hartmann (2006, EJOR): the best performing methods in their experiments are metaheuristics ('the best performing methods are metaheuristics').
Kolisch and Hartmann (2006, EJOR): adding forward-backward improvement to random sampling gives much better results than adding a priority rule.
Kolisch and Hartmann (2006, EJOR): neither the serial nor the parallel schedule generation scheme is consistently superior, so it appears a good idea to employ both.
Kolisch and Hartmann (2006, EJOR), 30 activities: the best method (Kochetov and Stolyar) is 0.10 %, 0.04 % and 0.00 % above the optimum after 1,000, 5,000 and 50,000 schedules.
Kolisch and Hartmann (2006, EJOR), 30 activities (Table 1, J30): a simple sampling rule is 0.30 to 0.54 % above the optimum at a budget of 1,000 schedules.
note: Instance size and schedule budget added from the paper text (Table 1, lines 455-490; the extracted row alignment is uncertain, so the range is as the collect file gives it).

claim: Kolisch and Hartmann (2006, EJOR), 60 activities (Table 2, J60): the best method (Debels et al., scatter search with forward-backward improvement) is 11.73, 11.10 and 10.71 % above the critical-path lower bound (not the optimum) after 1,000, 5,000 and 50,000 schedules.
note: The collect file calls this row 120 activities; the row (paper.txt line 546) is in Table 2, set J = 60 (caption line 623). Schedule budgets added from the table header.

claim: Kolisch and Hartmann (2006, EJOR), 60 activities (Table 2, J60): the 12.75, 11.90 and 11.54 % row (Bouleimen and Lecocq, one of the two benchmark heuristics of the earlier survey) is above the critical-path lower bound, not the optimum, after 1,000, 5,000 and 50,000 schedules.
note: The collect file calls this row 120 activities; the row (paper.txt line 557) is in Table 2, set J = 60. Schedule budgets added from the table header.

claim: Dean and Ghemawat (2004, Google, self-reported): backup executions near the end of a MapReduce operation typically increase the resources used by no more than a few percent.
Dean and Ghemawat (2004, Google, self-reported): a bad disk (read performance slowed from 30 MB/s to 1 MB/s) is one of the named causes of stragglers in MapReduce.
note: Wording at collect line 56 is '(30 MB/s to 1 MB/s)'; the paper (txt line 157) says a bad disk with frequent correctable errors may slow its read performance from 30 MB/s to 1 MB/s.

claim: Dean and Ghemawat (2004, Google, self-reported): a cache bug slowed work 'by over a factor of one hundred' in one of the named straggler causes.
Dean and Ghemawat (2004, Google, self-reported, one benchmark): the sort program takes 44 % longer to complete when the backup task mechanism is disabled.
Dean and Ghemawat (2004, Google, self-reported): the sort's last five reduce tasks finish 300 seconds after the rest, so the whole computation takes 1283 seconds, 44 % more elapsed time.
note: The 960 s and 300 s figures are from txt line 344.

claim: Zaharia et al. (2008, LATE): the scheduler always speculatively executes the task it thinks will finish farthest into the future.
Zaharia et al. (2008, LATE): time left is estimated as (1 - ProgressScore)/ProgressRate, which assumes tasks make progress at a roughly constant rate.
note: A stated condition: constant progress rate.

claim: Zaharia et al. (2008, LATE): the SpeculativeCap is set to 10 % of available task slots, and the slow-node and slow-task thresholds to the 25th percentile.
Zaharia et al. (2008, LATE): in a sensitivity analysis on a sleep workload, the optimal value for SpeculativeCap was 20 %, larger than the 10 % used in the EC2 evaluation.
note: Checked at paper.txt lines 586 and 588; the collect line 66 says 'found 20 % best'.

claim: Zaharia et al. (2008, LATE): LATE improves Hadoop response times by a factor of 2 in clusters of 200 virtual machines on EC2.

Zaharia et al. (2008, LATE): on a 30 GB sort with 486 map and 437 reduce tasks over 6 runs on shared virtual machines, LATE finished jobs 27 % faster than Hadoop's native scheduler and 31 % faster than no speculation.

Zaharia et al. (2008, LATE), four experiments with induced stragglers: LATE was 58 % faster than Hadoop's native scheduler, 220 % faster than Hadoop with speculative execution disabled, and up to 93 % faster.
Google's own figure, quoted by Zaharia et al. (2008, LATE): speculative execution can improve job response times by 44 % (self-reported).
note: The 44 % is Google's self-reported figure as LATE cites it (its reference [1]); it is not measured by Zaharia et al.

claim: Ananthanarayanan et al. (2010, Mantri; Microsoft Bing, self-reported): outliers inflate the completion time of jobs by 34 % at the median.
Ananthanarayanan et al. (2010, Mantri): a task that runs for long because it has more work to do is not restarted ('will not be restarted').

Ananthanarayanan et al. (2010, Mantri; Microsoft Bing, self-reported): Mantri reduced the completion time of jobs by 32 % on average on the production clusters, measured as June runs against April-May runs of the same jobs on the earlier build (a before-and-after comparison).
note: Narrowed after refute A66 (paper.txt line 1009). The rest of the sentence at line 32 was cut in the text extraction; the other evaluation figures were not recovered.

claim: Ananthanarayanan et al. (2013, Dolly): stragglers are on average 8 times slower than the median task in their job and increase the average job duration by 47 %.

Ananthanarayanan et al. (2013, Dolly; 150-node cluster replaying Facebook and Bing traces): cloning improved the average completion time of small jobs by 34 % against LATE and 46 % against Mantri, with a resource budget of 5 %.
note: The paper reads 'respectively, with LATE and Mantri as baselines', so 34 % goes with LATE and 46 % with Mantri.

claim: Ananthanarayanan et al. (2013, Dolly): cloning reduced the slowest task from running 8 times slower on average to 1.06 times.
Ananthanarayanan et al. (2013, Dolly): the cloning budget operates within an allotted resource budget, a configurable fraction (beta) of the total capacity.
Lifka (1995, ANL/IBM SP scheduling system): 'a FIFO queue was extremely inefficient' on the SP.
note: Mechanism only: the paper has no utilisation or wait figures.

claim: Lifka (1995, ANL/IBM SP scheduling system): backfilling fills idle nodes with later queued jobs, provided they do not cause the first queued job to wait any longer for the nodes it requires.
note: Mechanism only: the paper has no utilisation or wait figures.
